RCMP Report On Marijuana Trafficking Contradicts The Party Line
About Marijuana Smuggling From Canada To DEAland. Far More Goes North Than South

It is relatively easy to estimate the annual volume of hashish reaching the Canadian market. Unlike drugs such as cocaine and marihuana, which can be found everywhere in Canada and the United States, hashish consumption is a localized phenomenon in North America. While it is popular in Quebec, Ontario and in the Atlantic provinces, demand is limited elsewhere in Canada and supplies appear to be sporadic at best in the northeastern United States. Montreal-based organized crime groups have consequently specialized in the large-scale importation of hashish and exercise a monopoly over its wholesale distribution. Based on the preceding factors and intelligence on multi-tonne hashish shipments seized in Canada and abroad and those known to have entered the Canadian market, analysts estimate that at least 100 tonnes of this drug enter Canada every year.

In November 1998, a two year investigation was concluded with the interception of 15 tonnes of hashish on Canada’s West Coast. Most often, hashish is imported directly into Canada in multi- tonne shipments from Pakistan and Afghanistan. There have been cases where shipments transited the United States. There are no incidents of large-scale hashish smuggling to the United States from Canada, as this product is not sought after by U.S. drug users.

The hashish market in Central and eastern Canada is known world-wide. U.S. criminals are among the international traffickers that orchestrate multi-tonne shipments of this drug from Pakistan directly to Montreal by mothership or container.

Although liquid hashish (which is in fact processed marihuana) is manufactured in Canada, an estimated six to eight tonnes are imported yearly from Jamaica. Half that amount enters through Pearson International Airport in Toronto. The rest is imported by Canadian traffickers dealing with brokers based in Jamaica and Florida. The drugs are most often brought to Florida by small boats and then transported overland to Canada, particularly Southern Ontario. In April 1998, Canada Customs in Halifax detected a shipment of liquid hashish concealed in the structure of a boat cradle. Approximately 313 kilograms were recovered.

The RCMP estimates the annual production of marihuana in Canada to be at least in the 800 tonne range, a figure that equates to less than 60 grams per Canadian in the 15 to 45 year old category. This represents a harvest of 4.7 million plants, given that a mature plant yields on average 170 grams of marketable substance, i.e. flowering tops. This estimate appears overwhelming, however investigators believe it is quite conservative and that it is supported by intelligence and seizures of marihuana in plant and bulk forms. In 1998, over one million plants were seized across Canada by different police departments. Indoor hydroponic installations growing more than 3,000 plants are not an uncommon occurrence.
See

It is estimated that more than 50 % of the marihuana available in Canada is produced domestically. Mexican marihuana continues to enter Canada, however, usually via the United States.(Marijuananews note: This would mean that far more marijuana enters Canada from DEAland than moves South.)
See

In 1998, U.S. authorities seized Canada-bound marihuana shipments of various sizes totalling 3,800 kilograms.

Jamaica is another source of marihuana for the Canadian market. In March 1998, Canada Customs in Halifax discovered 1,474 kilograms of marihuana hidden in a marine container of produce arriving from Jamaica.

The smuggling of Canadian marihuana to the United States appears to be increasing, particularly from British Columbia. In 1994, an RCMP storefront currency exchange operation in that province established that over a three year period, more than $10 million dollars linked to the export of marihuana to the United States had passed through its offices. In June and July 1997, nearly $2 million in cash from marihuana transactions was seized from vehicles returning from the United States.

Despite the foregoing, few U.S. marihuana seizures can be traced back to Canada.

Although it is still a developing market, it is likely that marihuana is being smuggled into the United States across all land border points. Organized crime groups in the province of Quebec are supplying marihuana to their U.S. counterparts.
